Is Windows 10 bad? I'm being serious. My background, I'm a a Mac and Linux user. I've tried Windows 10 and I really think, so far, it is the best version of Windows they've made in quite some time.

I know there are some privacy issues, but you are going to get that with any OS connected to the Internet. Tons of guidance in this thread about different distributions, but if you've never used linux before don't get caught up in the details. The easiest dist to use IMO is Ubuntu. It is incredibly well supported, with a huge community. They don't strictly conform to GNU principles, but this is for the user benefit.

I used Linux exclusively for about two years while working another IT job. Like any OS, you get used to how it is laid out, and how it works. Pick a distribution you think most closely aligns with your goals and principles and start learning. The Linux community is very helpful, no question too dumb. Go out, break shit, and have fun, you'll learn the ins and outs quickly.

As a general rule of thumb with Windows -- pre-sp1/2 is always shit.

XP? Shit. Vista? Shit. 7? Ok but it was Vista with a new UI around the same time the SP came for Vista (what a coincidence?).

Many people don't remember Pre-Windows XP-SP2 and how annoying it was. SP2 made it fucking rock solid and ruled. Windows 7 was more like Vista SP2 + new Explorer.exe. Both are pretty rock solid.

Windows ME and 2K where two different philosophies. Windows 95 was their first real paradigm change from 3.X (and didn't change much until Vista came around which wasn't much of a change but spooked the people scared of change, and changed again with 8 with their Metro interface). Windows 98 and then 98SE where better but still had gaping security holes.

The problem is this: You go from a rock solid system that's tried and true to a new paradigm that isn't tried and tested.

What do you expect will happen? There will always be issues. Remember the old clunky smartphones that some people got mocked at for wearing on their hips 15 years ago? Those turned in to modern day phones you can't live without now. First-generation anything -- you're ALWAYS the beta tester. Period. Smart watches are in that phase right now.

Change will not guarantee that things will get better however doing nothing will guarantee they certainly won't. This is why we upgrade and change.

People flipped their shit with how much a "memory hog" Vista was without realizing they were foolish in their assumptions. Vista pre-loaded programs that you used often in an effort to get them loaded faster. Systems had more memory than every before and unsued memory is wasted memory. If needed, it would release that memory for use by other applications.

ctrl+F and I only see one mention of the best distribution for new users ever? Of course, I am talking about Linux Mint. But first, I'll tell you how I arrived at Linux Mint.

I had used Ubuntu since 7.10 (when GNOME was still its standard GUI), and I would still swear by Ubuntu if it hadn't switched to Unity. Honestly, KDE (before KDE 4) or GNOME 2.0 were probably the best GUIs. But now, they are both bloated. And as far as Unity goes? Forget it. I hate Unity, and I don't like that Ubuntu has that as default. Xubuntu, based on XFCE is a good alternative if you're REALLY set on Ubuntu. I had dabbled with it all the way up until about 12.04. It was a really good OS and Linux distribution.

But after about a few months of trying Ubuntu and other distros, I arrived at Linux Mint (which back in 2008 was based off of Ubuntu and Debian...now it's almost its own thing) and almost immediately, I fell in love with it. What I loved about it (and still love) is that its packages are basically interchangeable with Ubuntu's, as they're both Debian-based distros. So anything that worked for Ubuntu would work for Mint (but .mint packages won't work with Ubuntu necessarily; .deb packages will work for both), making support for it easier. If there was a problem with Mint, but I couldn't find it specifically for Mint, I could google the same problem but change "Mint" to "Ubuntu" and 90% of the time, if there was a solution for Ubuntu, it'd work for Mint too! But those are just the technical things that make me love Mint.

What really hooked me was that it looked and functioned more like Windows. Start menu and such. Now, you can even do wikipedia searches with the Mint menu! And Mint has a pretty sweet package manager (yes, it still does have Synaptic), but along with the great stuff you got from Ubuntu and Debian's package managers, it has something called "Software Manager" which allows you to search for applications or programs which suit your needs, and it has user reviews and ratings to go with it all. There are picture previews and everything!

It has gotten less easy to customize in recent editions, though, which has me somewhat bummed. Back when I started using Linux Mint, I was using Linux Mint 5 "Elyssa"; now it's on 17.2 or something. But whereas the old interface was GNOME-based, and you could customize the window color and text color and all that jazz with a color wheel thing in the settings, NOW you have to go straight into the files themselves and type in the hexcode values, which is why I hate that they've moved away from GNOME. I miss Compiz as well.

But it does have a lot of themes to choose from, right out of the box, and they're all pretty splendid. I'd really recommend giving Linux Mint a shot if you feel like Ubuntu's interface is too shitty.
It's worth noting that the Mate Edition uses something almost identical to Gnome.
